items.title: CoreWeave bond yield rises above 16% amid increasing credit stress in AI infrastructure sector [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises
items.summary:
CoreWeave's 2032 bond yield has surged past 16%, reflecting growing investor concern over financing risks in the AI data center market. Credit default swap costs have also increased for major AI-linked companies like Nvidia, Broadcom, and Oracle, signaling heightened default risk perceptions.

The rise in credit costs comes amid political challenges and potential moratoriums on data center expansions in key states such as Texas, Ohio, and Georgia, which could delay or reduce AI infrastructure spending. Despite these pressures, AI-related debt issuance remains robust, with significant borrowing expected to continue funding hyperscaler capital expenditures.

Market analysts warn that the sustainability of AI spending depends on future cash flow generation and timely monetization, with potential risks including delayed contracts and reduced capital expenditure. Forecasts suggest AI-related credit issuance may peak soon, with possible declines if infrastructure projects slow due to political or economic factors.

items.title: Simon Willison uses Claude Code to build Beep Locator, a Python web app triangulating a mysterious beep in a room using multiple devices and browser microphones [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.summary:
Simon Willison developed Beep Locator with Claude Code to identify the source of an intermittent beep in his house by triangulating sound using multiple devices like iPads, phones, and laptops connected via a Python web server. The system uses browser microphones and WebSockets to detect beeps, estimate device locations, and map the sound source to within about 40cm, ultimately locating a carbon monoxide detector needing new batteries.

Beep Locator is based on the 2007 BeepBeep acoustic ranging system paper and runs a Python server coordinating devices that record audio buffers and detect beeps using Fast Fourier Transform and high-pass filters. The system aligns audio clips using chirps played by devices, supports manual rough positioning of devices, and includes features like clapping mode for testing and replaying recorded sounds to confirm the beep source.

The project demonstrates how Claude Code can be extended with audio input capabilities by running JavaScript and Python code analyzing microphone data across devices, enabling remote live code updates and interactive debugging without manual intervention on each listener device.

items.originalSummary:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

items.title: Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with improved coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities, faster output, and enhanced safety features [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
items.summary:
Anthropic has upgraded its Claude Fable and Claude Mythos models to version 5.2, enhancing their abilities in coding, reasoning, and vision tasks. These models have demonstrated success in complex technical challenges such as software migrations, device design, physics problem-solving, robotics, and formal mathematical proofs. Claude Fable 5.2 includes robust cybersecurity and biology safeguards, making it broadly available, while Mythos 5.2 is accessible through specialized programs for life sciences and cybersecurity research.

The new versions communicate more clearly and generate outputs up to 30% faster than their predecessors, with an optional fast mode that increases speed by up to 2.5 times at higher pricing. Extensive prerelease safety testing indicates that these models maintain or improve alignment and safety measures, including protections against misuse and distillation attacks. Anthropic recommends using Claude Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge tasks, reserving Fable and Mythos 5.2 for more ambitious technical work or as advisors and orchestrators in multi-model workflows.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, highest among comparable models despite high cost and slow speed [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 on Artificial Analysis, highest so far
items.summary:
Claude Fable 5.2, a proprietary AI model released in November 2026, achieved a score of 65 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, significantly above the median score of 40 for similar models. It supports text and image inputs with a 1 million token context window but is noted for its high cost and slower performance compared to peers.

The model's pricing is $8.00 per 1 million input tokens and $40.00 per 1 million output tokens, making it more expensive than the median rates of $2.00 and $10.00 respectively. It also takes an average of 46.4 minutes per task, which is considerably slower than the median of 12.6 minutes. Claude Fable 5.2 is also very verbose, generating 275 million tokens during evaluation compared to a median of 72.8 million.

items.title: Google confirms Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human reviewers despite earlier privacy promises [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
items.summary:
Google has updated its policies to disclose that its Gemini AI system routes personal content from Gmail and Drive to human annotators, reversing its 2023 promise that such data would not be seen by humans. Testing shows that Gemini autonomously accesses and ingests personal files and emails during conversations without explicit user commands, sometimes including sensitive information in the review pipeline.

The ingestion process is probabilistic, with outcomes ranging from no data retrieval to full unredacted file ingestion. Google warns users not to connect apps containing confidential information to Gemini, as automatic scrubbers cannot fully deidentify personal data. This change raises concerns about privacy and the extent of human review in AI-assisted Workspace integrations.

items.title: Meta launches Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient AI model for complex reasoning and agent tasks, offering higher intelligence per cost than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Muse Ember: Our smallest, most efficient model
items.summary:
Meta introduced Muse Ember, a compact and efficient AI model designed for complex reasoning tasks such as tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. It delivers superior intelligence per dollar compared to Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna, matching or exceeding their performance at significantly lower costs. Muse Ember is available via the Meta Model API with pricing set at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.

The model supports a 1 million token context window and up to 512,000 output tokens, enabling it to process entire codebases or document sets in a single call. Early testing by partners highlighted its speed, accuracy, and efficiency in tasks like contract review, candidate screening, and coding, with latency significantly lower than comparable models. Muse Ember also natively understands multiple modalities including text, images, audio, and video, allowing it to handle diverse real-world inputs without separate models.

Designed for high-throughput agentic workloads, Muse Ember excels at repetitive, structured tasks agents perform throughout the day. It is positioned as a cost-effective foundation for enterprise AI agents handling workflows end to end, and it can be paired with Meta's larger Muse Wonder model for more complex problem-solving.

items.title: Research develops a prototype case-based reasoning system to enhance academic advising and potentially replace human advisors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
items.summary:
This research explores the application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) to academic advising, a critical but time-consuming function in higher education. The study presents the design, development, and validation of a prototype CBR-based academic advisement recommender system intended to supplement traditional advising processes and improve their effectiveness and efficiency.

The prototype aims to address the widespread need for improved advisement services in colleges and universities worldwide by leveraging CBR expert system methodologies, which have been successful in other problem-solving domains but have not yet been applied effectively to academic advising. The system could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors as its capabilities mature.

items.title: Researchers introduce NormGym benchmark to evaluate AI agents' ability to infer and apply hidden social norms through interaction, finding current large language models achieve only 55.3% success [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
items.summary: NormGym is an interactive benchmark designed to test normative competence, where AI agents must infer hidden social norms while completing tasks in multi-agent environments. The benchmark challenges agents to distinguish permissible actions from possible ones by observing behaviors and sanctions within the community. Evaluation of current models, including large language models, shows that while they can sometimes adjust behavior after personal sanctions, they struggle to infer norms from others' actions and sanctions, with the best model achieving just over half success in combined task and compliance metrics. The study also finds that fine-tuning alone may not significantly improve normative competence, indicating a gap in AI's ability to acquire transferable social norms through interaction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. Success requires distinguishing what is possible from what is permitted, inferring the norm from observed behavior and sanctions, and applying it in new situations. NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents. We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Our analysis reveals that models can sometimes revise their behavior following sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to use other agents' behavior and the sanctions they receive to infer the underlying norm. We further find that fine-tuning models may be insufficient to improve normative competence. These results suggest that current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.

items.title: Researchers propose LLM-based feature extraction to integrate unstructured customer feedback into multi-criteria inventory classification, enhancing prioritization in e-commerce supply chains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
items.summary: Researchers propose a method using large language models (LLMs) to extract quantitative features from unstructured data like customer reviews for multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) in e-commerce supply chains. Traditional methods rely mainly on structured data such as annual dollar usage, but this approach incorporates sentiment and other unstructured signals into the Hadi-Vencheh MCIC framework. Experimental results demonstrate that including customer sentiment leads to measurable changes in inventory classification, suggesting that leveraging unstructured data can improve inventory management decisions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.

items.title: Researchers introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for test-time selection in LLMs, improving candidate solution choice by comparing options across multiple aspects without training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for Test-Time Selection
items.summary:
Researchers propose Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), a method for selecting the best candidate solution generated by large language models (LLMs) at test time. APT compares candidate solutions pairwise across multiple aspects using off-the-shelf verifiers, mimicking human decision-making by evaluating options aspect by aspect rather than in isolation. This approach improves performance over existing methods like binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency, and reward model verification, especially on open-ended tasks.

APT operates as a single-elimination tournament where each matchup is decided by votes from multiple aspect verifiers, all specified in natural language. This design allows users to steer selection toward desired properties without retraining or regenerating solutions. The method transfers easily to new domains by rewriting prompts, requiring no additional training, and has been tested across five domains and three LLM generators with consistent improvements.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. A popular method is best-of-n sampling, where a model generates many candidate solutions and one is selected. This motivates the question: how can we select the best candidate? When humans make choices, we find it more natural to compare two options than judge each in isolation. Additionally, when the options become complex, we like to judge the options one aspect at a time, such as comparing two job candidates on experience, communication, etc. In the test-time setting, candidate solutions should be judged in the same way. Here we introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), which verifies by comparison and compares by aspect. Each matchup of a single elimination tournament is decided by a vote over multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers, each expressing a pairwise preference along its own aspect. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, APT improves over binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward model verification, with the largest gains on open-ended tasks. We find that both components matter; neither binary approval over the same aspects nor a generic pairwise judge at a matched budget matches APT. Because aspects are specified in natural language, APT also lets users steer selection toward properties they care about, better aligning with user preferences without needing to regenerate solutions. No component is trained, so APT transfers to new domains by simply rewriting prompts.

items.title: Researchers present Forge Decision Context system to enable persistent behavioral learning in AI agents, improving compliance to 95% on a new benchmark with fewer tokens [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
items.summary: Researchers introduce Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system designed to help large language model agents learn from human corrections and self-assessed failures across sessions by converting behavioral signals into imperative rules applied at relevant decision points. Evaluated on DC-Bench, a benchmark with 71 scenarios covering nine behavioral dimensions, forge_dc achieved 95% compliance compared to 55% with naive retrieval, while using about ten times fewer tokens per query. The study highlights that representing behavioral memory as explicit directives and delivering them at decision points are key design factors for effective persistent behavioral learning in AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.

items.title: IWIBench benchmarks large editor models modifying smaller target models' weights without gradients across ten text-editing tasks, revealing uneven capabilities among leading models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
items.summary:
IWIBench is introduced as a benchmark to evaluate how well large editor models can modify the weights of smaller target models directly, without using gradients, to achieve various text-editing objectives while preserving other model functions. The benchmark tests ten classical editing tasks using limited tools and a fixed rollout budget, with a validator comparing edited models to unmodified versions in a clean environment. Evaluation of frontier closed- and open-weight models shows significant differences in performance across models and tasks, with Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol notably outperforming others, suggesting recent training improvements.

Tasks vary in difficulty, with alias acquisition and recoding being more amenable to editing, while structured response and answer-length control proved challenging. Success in one task family does not strongly correlate with others, indicating an early and uneven development of intra-weight injection capabilities. The study discusses common editing strategies and positions intra-weight injection as a promising gradient-free method for modifying model behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.

items.title: Researchers compare debugger-only and bash-only coding agents on 500 SWE-bench instances using GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B models, introducing pass$_X$@$k$ to measure success probability across agents
items.originalTitle: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
items.summary: Researchers evaluated the effectiveness of interactive debuggers versus bash tools for coding agents by comparing a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, using two large language models with multiple runs. They introduced pass$_X$@$k$, a metric estimating the probability that at least one of k agents succeeds, to distinguish interface specialization from sampling variance. The study found that differences in solved subsets were mainly due to run-to-run variance rather than complementary tool capabilities, with two bash rollouts outperforming a combination of bash and debugger rollouts. These findings emphasize the need to account for stochastic variance when assessing agent and tool diversity and propose pass$_X$@$k$ as a useful evaluation framework for the community.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. To address this, we compare a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, holding the rest of the scaffold fixed. We evaluate both architectures on two models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, with three independent runs per architecture $\times$ model configuration. Crucially, to distinguish interface specialization from expanded coverage under repeated sampling, we introduce pass$_X$@$k$, a cross-agent pass@$k$ that provides an unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of $k$ agents is successful. Although the bash and debugger agents solve partially disjoint subsets of the benchmark in any single pair of runs, our pass$_X$@$2$ estimator reveals that this is largely due to run-to-run variance rather than tool complementarity. Across both models, we find that two bash rollouts outperform the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic variance in evaluating agent and tool diversity, and we hope that pass$_X$@$k$ will serve as a useful framework for the community.

items.title: ChainFlow introduces a flow-matching drafter for speculative decoding that outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash on Qwen3.5 models by up to 39%, improving LLM inference speed [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
ChainFlow is a new speculative decoding method that accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target model's hidden states. Unlike existing drafters that either generate tokens one at a time or predict tokens independently, ChainFlow performs drafting as a short transport over hidden states with one or two flow steps, reducing computational cost and preserving inter-token dependencies.

The approach uses a variational autoencoder to compress hidden states, lightweight feedback heads to restore token dependencies, and tree drafting to increase acceptance rates. On Qwen3.5 models, ChainFlow achieves 39% and 11% speed improvements over EAGLE-3 and DFlash drafters in vLLM, respectively, with gains increasing as drafters adapt to new languages. The authors provide ablation studies on drafter design and concurrent serving and have open-sourced their code and models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.

items.title: Researchers propose two optimal transport frameworks for backtracking counterfactual inference in Structural Causal Models, addressing exogenous variable distributions and independence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Transporting the Past: An Optimal Transport View of Backtracking Counterfactuals
items.summary:
This paper studies backtracking counterfactual inference in Structural Causal Models (SCMs) using optimal transport methods. The authors introduce two frameworks that map the posterior distribution of exogenous variables, induced by factual observations, onto configurations satisfying counterfactual queries. One framework uses a pointwise projection suitable for direct use of the transported distribution, while the other enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables to maintain their interpretability as genuine noises of the SCM.

The study demonstrates that both frameworks align with the original backtracking counterfactual principle and proposes several solvers for finite-posterior scenarios. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the problem's geometry and highlight trade-offs between transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study backtracking counterfactual inference for Structural Causal Models (SCMs) through the lens of optimal transport. In SCMs, a factual observation generally induces a posterior distribution over exogenous variables, making counterfactual inference inherently distributional. We introduce two complementary frameworks that transport this posterior onto the set of exogenous configurations satisfying a desired counterfactual query. The first constructs a natural pointwise projection and is suitable when the transported exogenous distribution can be used directly. The second enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables, so that the transported variables remain interpretable as genuine exogenous noises of the same SCM. We show that both frameworks are consistent with the original backtracking counterfactual principle, and we propose marginal, penalty-based, and hard-constrained solvers for finite-posterior settings. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the geometry of the problem and reveal trade-offs among transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.

items.title: Researchers find cancellation alone fails to restore service in overloaded vLLM engines with retries, delivering only 12-38% of calls after overload [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cancellation Is Not Enough: What Retries Leave Behind in an Overloaded LLM Engine
items.summary:
Researchers tested cancellation and retry mechanisms on vLLM during overload experiments with three open models, tracking client attempts and engine executions. They found that retries often started shortly before timeout, leading to aborted executions that consumed most computed prompt tokens, while cancellation alone did not restore service and delivered a minority of calls after overload.

The study showed that implementing a retry budget improved service by limiting retries but left many calls undelivered, whereas request coalescing delivered all calls post-overload unless cancellation had aborted execution. The findings suggest that overload controls should consider the additional executions caused by retries and the actual calls clients receive rather than relying solely on cancellation propagation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clients and proxies in front of an LLM engine retry calls that time out. After a transient overload, these retries can keep the engine from recovering even when calls arrive below its capacity. Since the engine may keep computing for clients that have left, propagating cancellation looks like the natural remedy. In this paper, we test it on vLLM with overload experiments on three open models, and with scheduler traces of one that follow each client attempt to the execution it creates in the engine. We find that with retries on, cancellation alone did not restore service in any run, and only 12-38% of the calls that arrived after the overload were delivered. The traces suggest why: retries that vLLM ran typically started prefill less than half a second before they timed out. Executions that vLLM later aborted took 79-85% of the prompt tokens it computed, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to half of all computed prompt tokens. A retry budget restored service by shedding retries but left many of the overload's calls undelivered. Request coalescing delivered every call from the overload onward, some late, unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution. Overload controls should thus be judged by the executions that retries add and the calls that clients receive.

items.title: Researchers propose memory-aware multi-agent architecture with LLM-based orchestration for conversational recommendation, improving intent tracking and user acceptance in Amazon Reviews dataset experiments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
items.summary:
Researchers propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation systems, where large language models (LLMs) orchestrate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow while integrating long-term memory to better capture evolving user intent. The system was evaluated on the Amazon Reviews dataset through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn simulations, and supervisor-driven studies, showing that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and increase user acceptance by nearly 29 percentage points.

The study also identifies an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations, noting that while LLM-based reranking does not improve traditional Hit@K metrics, it enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To better measure these effects, the researchers introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), emphasizing the importance of system-level design choices such as explicit memory integration, structured orchestration, and evaluation beyond standard ranking metrics for effective conversational recommendation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.

items.title: AttentionSwitch jointly optimizes sparse attention-head selection and scaling to defend frozen large language models against jailbreak attacks, improving safety with limited training data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
items.summary: AttentionSwitch introduces a novel approach to defending large language models (LLMs) from jailbreak attacks by jointly learning which attention heads to intervene on and how to scale their outputs within a frozen model. This method allows selective amplification or attenuation of attention head outputs without changing their representation directions, addressing limitations of prior sequential optimization defenses. Evaluated across popular LLMs and jailbreak scenarios, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing methods, particularly when training data is scarce, offering a computationally efficient alternative to fine-tuning that avoids catastrophic forgetting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.

items.title: Researchers propose Debate-to-Deceive, a multi-agent game-theoretic framework that generates adversarial passages to poison LLM fact-checking, outperforming existing attacks on four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework inspired by human rhetorical styles, designed to manipulate fact-checking judgments of large language models (LLMs). D2D models the adversarial process as an evolutionary game where agents adapt rhetorical strategies to produce semantically coherent and rhetorically effective adversarial content that resists early confirmation bias.

D2D separates agent behavior into a strategic layer that selects rhetorical actions via evolutionary learning and a generation layer where the LLM produces passages based on these strategies and debate context. Evaluated on four fact-checking benchmarks—FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact—D2D significantly outperforms prior attack methods and evades most existing defenses, highlighting new challenges for AI reliability and robustness in fact-checking tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge attacks on Large Language Models, such as manipulating fact-checking judgments, pose significant risks to AI reliability. Existing approaches -- adversarial suffix/template injection and single-agent self-reflection -- lack robustness across diverse defenses and are prone to confirmation bias and costly trial-and-error, respectively. We propose Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework grounded in human debate structure and rhetorical style, enabling agents to generate adversarial passages that are semantically coherent, rhetorically effective, and resistant to early confirmation bias. D2D formalizes the adversarial process as an evolutionary game in which agents adaptively evolve their rhetorical strategies (Logos, Pathos, Ethos) through competition. To manage the intractably large LLM output space, we decouple agent behavior into a strategic layer, which selects a rhetorical action from a compact strategy space via evolutionary-inspired learning dynamics, and a generation layer, where the LLM produces a concrete passage conditioned on that strategy and the debate context. On four fact-checking benchmarks (FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact), D2D substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses.

items.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
items.originalTitle: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

items.title: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while retaining memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. We introduce a control-theoretic framework that couples a fast loop controlling proposed actions with a slow loop reviewing persistent changes and reassessing configurations after model or tool updates. When measurement errors and changes between checks are bounded and controllers can enforce their decisions, we derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort. In simulation, dividing a fixed review budget between both loops reduces mean maximum departure from intended behavior roughly twelvefold compared with review confined to individual runs. In coding stress tests with authored memories and five matched seeds, combined controls reduce mean severity on a 0-3 scale from 0.325 without gates to 0.117, resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates; in trading stress tests, combined controls reduce mean shortfall in low-emission purchases from 0.892 without gates to 0.107. The overall framework helps developers and auditors compare and enforce oversight designs, while the agent studies test component controls rather than the full deployment-level guarantee.

items.title: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) remains central -and debated- in binary classification. This survey offers a comprehensive retrospective and an in-depth analysis of MCC, covering its historical development, mathematical foundations, and implications for practice. We clarify long-standing misconceptions, formalize its equivalences (to Pearson's correlation and to Chi2 in 2x2 tables), and examine its behavior under class imbalance. Beyond MCC, we develop analytical (derivatives) and graphical (contour plots) frameworks that generalize to any confusion-matrix-based metric. These frameworks expose structural properties -bias, robustness, sensitivity- that scalar summaries conceal, and they provide actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting performance measures in applications where reliability and fairness matter. Together, our results position MCC within a broader toolkit while clarifying when it is informative -and when alternatives may be preferable.

items.title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). items.title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.

items.title: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equivalent encodings of an optimization problem can produce different learned predictions. Interpreting these differences requires accounting for numerical error and multiple optima. We construct metamorphic tests for optimization solver surrogates with explicit eligibility conditions, output alignment, and numerical thresholds. Reference-solver agreement and independent constraint checks determine which sampled pairs enter the audit. We study alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF), the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), and maximum independent set (MIS). Across five grids, GridSFM-Open violates each of 13 relations on at least one grid, and 12 by more than twice the threshold. Randomly initialized copies of the grid models fail nearly the same relations, so the failures do not require training. Source patches and input canonicalization remove selected discrepancies, but no intervention establishes preserved accuracy and feasibility within the declared margin on every grid. In routing, Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) has a single-pass rotation/reflection violation rate that rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities. Graph-Based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization (DIFUSCO) violates the MIS disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of draws. Post hoc normalization within connected components removes these violations on the tested graphs. These findings support reporting metamorphic consistency alongside optimality, feasibility, and accuracy, and validating repair quality separately from consistency.

items.title: When F1 Is Not Enough: Auditing Codebooks for LLM-Assisted Annotation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When F1 Is Not Enough: Auditing Codebooks for LLM-Assisted Annotation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation in social science, but standard performance metrics do not explain why errors occur. Low F1 may reflect limitations of the annotation system, defects in the written codebook, or inconsistency in reference labels. We propose a pre-deployment codebook audit for LLM-assisted annotation. The audit uses class-specific metrics and confusion matrices to identify problematic classes and boundaries, structured document-level review to attribute error sources, and targeted codebook revision followed by held-out evaluation. We apply the audit to two published multi-class codebooks from distinct domains. In both applications, the audit identifies under-specified or conflicting coding rules, and targeted revisions reduce the diagnosed errors on held-out data. Analyses with two LLM annotators show that some problematic boundaries and codebook revisions transfer across models, whereas other revision effects are annotator-specific. The results show that LLM annotation errors can help identify weaknesses in the written measurement instrument, not only in the model. Codebook auditing complements prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning by clarifying whether persistent errors call for model improvement, codebook revision, or renewed scrutiny of reference labels.

items.title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
items.originalTitle: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. Whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or the low prior credence of spiritual claims is the question the design leaves open, and we outline the experiment that would settle it.

items.title: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) integrates textual, acoustic, and visual cues to identify utterance-level emotions. However, existing approaches generally do not explicitly adapt multimodal processing to the degree of inter-modal predictive disagreement. In real conversations, semantic incongruity, concealed emotion, noisy observations, and ambiguity can affect modality-specific emotional evidence differently, while the reliability of individual modalities varies across samples. Rather than identifying each source of inconsistency separately, we model their common consequence for emotion recognition as predictive disagreement among unimodal emotion distributions over the same emotion-label set. Such disagreement makes indiscriminate fusion prone to propagating unreliable or competing evidence. Inspired by the Brunswik Lens Model, we propose MiD-ERC, a divergence-centric framework that quantifies inter-modal predictive disagreement using a normalized divergence score and estimates sample-specific modality reliability. MiD-ERC uses these signals to coordinate divergence-guided cross-modal gating, divergence-modulated reliability weighting, and divergence-conditioned adaptive LLM prompting. The framework is trained end-to-end using only standard emotion annotations, without requiring additional conflict labels, auxiliary data construction, or external retrieval modules. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD demonstrate that MiD-ERC achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly pronounced improvements on high-divergence samples.

items.title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.

items.title: Toward LLM Self-Play Under Data Scarcity: Effectiveness, Generalizability, and Trustworthiness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Toward LLM Self-Play Under Data Scarcity: Effectiveness, Generalizability, and Trustworthiness
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has been driven largely by scaling model size and human-curated training data, yet this paradigm is increasingly constrained by data scarcity and diminishing returns from human supervision. Self-play offers a promising pathway for autonomous data generation and improvement, but current frameworks remain unsatisfactory due to a lack of a data-centric perspective, limited cross-domain generalization, and growing trustworthiness and security concerns. In this paper, we argue that real-world LLM self-play systems should achieve effectiveness, generalizability, and trustworthiness under data scarcity. To address these challenges, we outline three blue-sky research directions for future self-play systems: (1) data-centric self-play for effective experience generation, (2) generalizable self-play for open-world and unverifiable tasks, and (3) trustworthy self-play for reliable self-evolution. We further discuss research opportunities and solutions within each direction. This paradigm shift will establish a sustainable and safe AI ecosystem by transforming finite human knowledge into inexhaustible high-quality experience through self-play architectures.

items.title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many professional reports reuse the structure of prior editions while updating the content. We formalize this setting as form-restricted report generation: given a sample report and new grounding documents, generate a report that preserves the sample's form while accurately reflecting the new evidence. We introduce FRAME, a benchmark of 120 EDGAR- and arXiv-derived instances across Financial Quarterly, Financial Annual, Academic Simple, and Academic Complex categories, built with a temporal three-snapshot pipeline. We evaluate outputs with three human-validated metrics: structural similarity via semantic tree-edit distance, coverage via information unit recall, and faithfulness via claim-level grounding verification. Across five LLMs, open-source models nearly match proprietary models on structure but lag on coverage and faithfulness; all models perform better on financial than academic reports, and performance declines with longer outputs and more complex grounding.

items.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

items.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.

items.title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

items.title: Rethinking Optimization Methods for Hierarchical Feature Selection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Optimization Methods for Hierarchical Feature Selection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rare-event forecasting often depends on interpretable conjunctions: a single keyword, location, or temporal cue may be weak, while their joint occurrence can identify a meaningful precursor. Hierarchical-Task Numerical conjunctive feature Learning (HTNL) selects Numerical Conjunctive Features (NCFs) through a structured sparsity objective. However, the resulting optimization problem is challenging, making optimization design critical to its practical performance. We give a unified diagnosis of four HTNL optimization families: original majorization-minimization (MM), variational quadratic form (VQF), alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), and weighted group lasso (WGL). Our analysis distinguishes three key factors that jointly determine HTNL optimization behavior. First, VQF and MM are algebraically equivalent under matched variational updates and optimize a squared-penalty formulation. Second, ADMM optimizes the unsquared objective through consensus splitting; we replace its truncated FISTA proximal solver with a scalar bisection update (ADMM-Bisect) for more accurate treatment of near-threshold blocks. Third, WGL targets the same unsquared objective, while all methods face rapidly decaying active-set admission scores. Across two synthetic datasets and 11 civil-unrest and flu-surveillance tasks, VQF achieves the highest mean AUC with the most compact non-collapsing supports. ADMM-Bisect reduces measured runtime, while calibrated WGL avoids the empty-support failures of its original scale. Synthetic results further show how proximal accuracy, pruning, and search budget affect candidate recovery, especially for longer conjunctions. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.

items.title: SIMBAD: Spatio-Temporal Traffic Forecasting Robust to Aperiodicity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SIMBAD: Spatio-Temporal Traffic Forecasting Robust to Aperiodicity
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate traffic prediction is essential for urban planning but remains challenging due to the irregular patterns caused by unexpected events. While Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) effectively model periodic data, they often struggle with these aperiodic fluctuations. To address this, we propose SIMBAD, which improves generalization irregular patterns via two key mechanisms: 1) adaptive regulation of periodic signals to prioritize recent signals, and 2) dynamic spatial modeling that adjusts influence between connected nodes based on contextual relations. Built upon simple similarity metrics to adapt to aperiodic patterns, SIMBAD outperforms existing methods on real-world benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior performance in predicting unseen and irregular traffic events.

items.title: Scout Before You Route: Predicting Task Success and Token Count from a Small LLM Prefill [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Scout Before You Route: Predicting Task Success and Token Count from a Small LLM Prefill
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Routers typically choose a model per query by trading predicted correctness against cost. Most price each model at a fixed cost, as if every query used the same number of output tokens, but the output length of reasoning models varies by an order of magnitude across queries. When is per-query cost worth predicting? What factors drive cost? How cheaply can predictions be made? We predict both the success probability and the output length of candidate models from the prefill activations of a single small frozen LLM, the scout. With reasoning candidates, perfect per-query cost knowledge would save 29-61% of spending on eight of nine datasets, and much less with non-reasoning candidates on the same problems. On those eight datasets, our predicted costs save 9-33% at matched accuracy relative to median-length pricing, up to 69% of what perfect knowledge would save. They are significantly cheaper than each estimator we reimplemented or adapted from published work, including ZeroRouter and a MixLLM-style predictor, on a majority of datasets. Output length depends mostly on the problem. On most math and code datasets, harder problems are longer, so predicted success alone prices cost nearly as well. On knowledge and mixed-format datasets they are not, and predicted success falls well behind a probe trained on length. The probe keeps most of its saving with 20 labelled problems and transfers without labels to four of seven new benchmarks. On a mixture of all nine benchmarks, it saves 22% beyond pricing each benchmark at its own median length. Savings stop growing at about a 2B scout, so above 4B a larger scout costs more than it adds.
